observations.text: SP flew the traffic pattern stalls at the code desired for the Training Section, entering each stall under IP direction and completing the recovery with the IP executing part of the control inputs. Recognition of the first stall characteristics remained IP-prompted on all four patterns and did not reduce across the sortie, with altitude loss on the landing attitude stall exceeding 300 feet on two entries. Performance is marginal for the block; independent identification of stall onset and an unassisted recovery are expected in the following sorties.

SP entered the BREAK stall in the prescribed configuration and initiated the recovery on the first stall characteristics after the IP's verbal prompt, without any control input from the IP. Altitude deviation was held at 300 feet, at the code 1 limit, and no secondary stall developed. Recognition was delayed, but the recovery itself was flown entirely by SP. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP flew the base leg stall into the buffet in the appropriate configuration and began the recovery on the first stall characteristics without IP prompting. A momentary over-rotation was identified and corrected by SP in a timely manner, with the result of an altitude loss of 220 feet, between the code 3 and code 1 limits and without IP intervention. Landing gear and flap airspeed limits were respected throughout. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP flew all four traffic pattern stalls deliberately and according to the Techniques and Procedures Manual, initiating each recovery with the appearance of the first stall characteristics. Recoveries were accurate and prompt, with no secondary stall and no exceedance of the landing gear and flap airspeed limits, and altitude loss on the landing attitude stall was held within 120 feet. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP entered and recovered every traffic pattern stall exactly as prescribed by the Techniques and Procedures Manual, with the recovery initiated at the first indication of stall onset on each entry. BREAK stall altitude deviation did not exceed 40 feet and the landing attitude stall was recovered with less than 50 feet of altitude loss, with no secondary stall and wide margins to the landing gear and flap airspeed limits. Control through the recovery met the Basic A/C Control criteria with minimum loss of altitude. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to a delayed and insufficient forward stick input at the stall break, did not execute the recovery procedure with the appearance of the first stall characteristics on the landing attitude stall. The IP directed the recovery and applied part of the control inputs to unload the aircraft, with the result that altitude loss exceeded 300 feet. Control through the recovery did not meet the Basic A/C Control criteria of minimum loss of altitude.

SP, due to the startle effect at the onset of the departure from controlled flight, did not apply the prescribed recovery actions on the BREAK stall and allowed a secondary stall to appear. The IP took control to complete the recovery, with the result of an altitude deviation beyond 300 feet. The stall series could not be flown deliberately, according to the Techniques and Procedures Manual, without IP assistance.

SP flew the traffic pattern stalls within the standards desired for the Training Section, initiating each recovery only after the IP's verbal prompt at the first stall characteristics. Recognition of stall onset was late on the overshooting (nose-low) final turn stall, and altitude loss on the landing attitude stall reached 300 feet, at the code 1 limit. No secondary stall appeared and no landing gear or flap airspeed limit was exceeded. Marginal performance for the Training Section; earlier and unprompted recognition of the first stall characteristics is expected to improve in the following sorties.

SP entered the BREAK stall deliberately and in the appropriate configuration and initiated the recovery on the first stall characteristics without IP prompting. A late relaxation of back pressure was recognized and corrected by SP in a timely manner, with the result of an altitude deviation of 210 feet, inside the code 1 limit and without IP intervention. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP flew the BREAK, base leg and landing attitude stalls according to the Techniques and Procedures Manual, recovering on the first stall characteristics at every entry. Execution was accurate and prompt, with BREAK stall altitude deviation within 130 feet, no secondary stall and no exceedance of the landing gear and flap airspeed limits. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP executed the full traffic pattern stall series with exceptional accuracy, entering each stall at the altitude prescribed by the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs and recovering at the first indication of buffet. BREAK stall altitude deviation stayed within 40 feet and the landing attitude stall was recovered with less than 50 feet of altitude loss, with no secondary stall at any point. Airspeed remained well inside the landing gear and flap limits throughout the sequence. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to an incorrect power and pitch sequence during the recovery, did not fly the landing attitude stall according to the Techniques and Procedures Manual and allowed a secondary stall to appear. The IP took control and completed the recovery, with the result of an altitude loss beyond 300 feet. The appropriate action for a secondary stall was not taken by SP.

SP, due to incomplete knowledge of the limits applicable to the maneuver, lowered the nose without reducing power on the recovery from the overshooting (nose-low) final turn stall and did not respect the airspeed limits of the landing gear and flaps. The IP intervened to arrest the acceleration and directed the remainder of the recovery, with the result of an altitude loss beyond 300 feet. The maneuver could not be completed to standard without IP assistance.

SP, due to a rushed entry that left the aircraft outside the appropriate configuration, did not fly the base leg stall deliberately according to the Techniques and Procedures Manual and identified the first stall characteristics only after the IP's verbal prompt. The recovery was then flown by SP without IP control input, with the result of an altitude loss of 300 feet, at the code 1 limit. The entry parameters were recognized and corrected with delay.

SP, due to failure to monitor the aircraft state after the configuration change, did not recognize the first stall characteristics on the BREAK stall and held the entry attitude past the buffet. The recovery was completed by SP after the IP's verbal prompts, with the result of an altitude deviation of 300 feet, at the code 1 limit, and a correction made with delay. No secondary stall appeared.

SP performed the traffic pattern stalls within the desired standards, entering each stall in the appropriate configuration and recovering on the first stall characteristics without IP intervention. Two small pitch control errors during the recovery were recognized and corrected by SP in a timely manner, with landing attitude stall altitude loss of 250 feet, close to the code 1 limit. Marginal performance for the Training Section; a wider margin on recovery altitude loss is expected to improve in the following sorties.

SP flew the four traffic pattern stalls deliberately and in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual, initiating each recovery with the appearance of the first stall characteristics and without IP prompting. Execution was accurate and prompt, with BREAK stall altitude deviation within 140 feet, no secondary stall and no exceedance of the landing gear and flap airspeed limits. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP executed the traffic pattern stall series with exceptional precision, holding the entry altitude prescribed by the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs and recovering at the very first stall indication on each maneuver. BREAK stall altitude deviation did not exceed 35 feet and the base leg stall was recovered with under 50 feet of altitude loss, with no secondary stall and wide margins to the landing gear and flap airspeed limits. Recovery control met the Basic A/C Control criteria with minimum loss of altitude. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to an abrupt and excessive back stick input at the entry, did not fly the undershooting (nose-high) final turn stall according to the Techniques and Procedures Manual and allowed a secondary stall after the initial recovery. The IP took control and completed the recovery, with the result of an altitude loss beyond 300 feet. The appropriate action for the secondary stall was not taken by SP.

SP, due to failure to recognise the undesired aircraft state before it developed further, did not initiate the recovery with the appearance of the first stall characteristics on the landing attitude stall and allowed the sink rate to increase. The IP directed the recovery and applied part of the control inputs, with the result of an altitude loss beyond 300 feet. The recovery did not meet the Basic A/C Control criteria of minimum loss of altitude.

SP, due to a trim setting carried over from the previous pattern, did not enter the BREAK stall at the altitude prescribed by the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs and flew the entry high. Recovery on the first stall characteristics followed only after the IP's verbal prompts, with the result of an altitude deviation of 300 feet, at the code 1 limit. The error was recognized and corrected with delay, without IP control input.

SP, due to stress that narrowed the scan to the parameter being evaluated, did not identify the first stall characteristics on the base leg stall and maintained the entry input past the buffet. The recovery was completed by SP after the IP's verbal prompts, with the result of an altitude loss of 300 feet, at the code 1 limit, and a correction made with delay. No secondary stall appeared and the landing gear and flap airspeed limits were not exceeded.

SP, due to a late reduction of power at the stall break, did not contain the acceleration on the recovery from the landing attitude stall as closely as the maneuver requires. The excursion was recognized and corrected by SP in a timely manner and without IP intervention, with the result of an altitude loss of 230 feet, between the code 3 and code 1 limits, and airspeed remaining inside the landing gear and flap limits. No secondary stall appeared.

SP, due to the startle effect at the onset of the departure from controlled flight, did not begin the recovery from the overshooting (nose-low) final turn stall at the first stall characteristics and delayed the initial control input. SP recognized the delay and completed the recovery without IP intervention, with the result of an altitude loss of 240 feet, between the code 3 and code 1 limits. The remaining stalls of the series were flown deliberately and to standard.

SP flew the traffic pattern stalls within the desired standards, entering each stall deliberately in the appropriate configuration and recovering on the first stall characteristics without IP intervention. Altitude loss on the base leg stall reached 145 feet, at the edge of the code 3 tolerance, and the climb after the landing attitude stall recovery was slow to establish. No secondary stall appeared and no landing gear or flap airspeed limit was exceeded. Marginal performance for the Training Section; a wider margin inside the 150 feet tolerance is expected in the following sorties.

SP executed all four traffic pattern stalls with exceptional accuracy, entering at the altitude prescribed by the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs and recovering at the first indication of stall onset on each entry. BREAK stall altitude deviation stayed within 30 feet, and both the base leg and the landing attitude stalls were recovered with less than 50 feet of altitude loss, with no secondary stall and wide margins to the landing gear and flap airspeed limits. Recovery control was flown to Basic A/C Control standards with minimum loss of altitude. Above end of block MIF achieved.
